crote · Nov 7, 2026

Sorry, but thousands of pushes per second, per repository?! In what world could that possibly seem like a sound idea?

Sure, it's nice that you can technically handle it, but to me it sounds like at that point something has gone absolutely horribly wrong in the way you set up your agents. Last time I checked, GitHub was intended as a platform to upstream finished work items, not a realtime cross-agent chat channel.

Handling thousands of git pushes per second implies thousands of issues, thousands of PRs, tens of thousands of comments, thousands of Actions runs, and dozens of releases. How's that part of their infra going to scale?

How about introducing rate limits instead, nudging people to not have agents push every individual single-line changes to GH, but instead have them collaborate as a local cluster and only upstreaming PR-sized chunks of finished work?

If you still need thousands of pushes per second you'd be looking at millions of lines of code, and at that point you're looking at an insane monorepo which is growing at a rate of terabytes per day, and which basically instantly becomes unusable due to being impossible to clone or check out.

> Sorry, but thousands of pushes per second, per repository?! In what world could that possibly seem like a sound idea?

The only conceivable scenario that I can imagine leading to this volume of writes is a push-based GitOps repository for a huge cluster holding a large volume of apps, each one with many services. Each commit in one if these services triggers a commit to the gitops repo to update the reference to the new container image, which in turns triggers a deployment update.

There is no software project on earth that justifies a rate of changes in magnitudes of dozen of commits per second. This is a symptom of a huge problem, not a sign of times. Even in monorepo mania this sort of thing is inconceivable.

But that's also what you get with vibecoding: lots of output from people who do not have a clue about what they are doing.

bob1029 · Nov 7, 2026

I think perforce might be the better VCS if you intend to have a bunch of autonomous agents attempt to collaborate over one big pile.

Multiple terabytes is no problem out of the box. You get exclusive locking of files. You can easily take partial checkouts of the monolith. Centralization is a feature in this particular context. Git works great if the need for coordination is moderate. If you've got thousands of automated developers with their hands in the cookie jar, exclusive locks start to look really compelling. Perforce sucks with a highly distributed team, but in the case of an AI agent swarm we presumably have the ability to instantly nuke an agent's checkout if needed. I don't have to contact the agent and wait for them to get out of bed.
